title: Northumberland pupils handle 4.3-billion-year-old meteorite and moon rocks
excerpt: Newbrough C of E Primary pupils handled rare meteorites, Martian rock and NASA moon rocks during STFC astronomy sessions on October 13 and 14 in Northumberland.

Primary school pupils have been given the chance to touch a piece of outer space.

Children at Newbrough C of E Primary School in Northumberland handled rare meteorites and moon rocks during two days of hands-on science sessions, held on October 13 and October 14.

The experience was part of an interactive astronomy programme supported by the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC).

Pupils were able to touch and examine genuine meteorites, including a 1.2-billion-year-old piece of Martian rock and a 4.3-billion-year-old nickel meteorite.

To put the age of the samples in context, Earth is estimated to be 4.6 billion years old.

The educational pack also included lunar material collected by NASA during its first manned missions to the moon in the late 1960s and early 1970s.

A total of 382kg of lunar material was brought back to Earth during these missions.

While most of it is reserved for scientific research, small amounts are used in educational packs like the one provided to Newbrough School.

Meteorites are fragments of rock from space that reach Earth’s surface.

The organisation hopes these packs will encourage students to become the next generation of astronomers.

The STFC is the only authorised body in the UK permitted to loan lunar samples to educational and scientific institutions.
